Subject: Capacity hedging proposal — Heliogenics Dedicated burst guardband

Hi Samantha / Tim,

Great meeting yesterday — thanks for the context on your inference peaks tied to training windows. To make the Dedicated capacity commitment work for both sides, we put together a short hedging proposal and an operational guardband for short-term bursts. High level:

- Baseline reserved slab: 40 GPUs (pinned to r-infer-v2) for steady-state throughput.
- Burst headroom: up to 65 GPUs available for ephemeral bursts (50% pre-warmed shoulder + opportunistic preemptible).
- Crediting model: 3 pre-approved burst windows per week (4 hours each) with automatic token-based credit deduction; additional bursts draw from an escrow bucket and trigger throttling at 80% queue depth.
- Autoscale policy: latency-first routing until 200ms p95, then degrade to lower-cost variant automatically; we’ll maintain a fallback model for non-critical pipelines.

I attached a runbook and a starting SLA draft for your legal/procurement review. Monica is looped on ops details; Karthik will draft the contractual language for credits & headroom.

Next steps proposed:
1) You confirm whether 65 GPU peak covers your maximum 5x traffic spike.
2) If yes, we’ll provide a simulated monthly cost delta and a runbook walkthrough next week.
3) Procurement: target signature by end of month to align with capacity planning for December.

1) The 5x spike is accurate for synchronous API traffic during model retrain/eval; worst-case sustained for ~3 hours.
2) We have another ML job that can cause short sub-minute bursts; would the autoscale policy handle short high-QPS bursts without consuming the weekly 4-hour windows?

Also, legal asked us to get explicit eviction behavior documented — if we go above 65 GPUs and Redwood needs to preempt, what signals do you surface to our app (headers/status codes) and how graceful is the degradation?

Subject: Re: Capacity hedging proposal — Heliogenics Dedicated burst guardband

Hi Samantha — quick ops response inline to your questions.

1) Short sub-minute bursts: We treat those as part of continuous batching windows. If a burst is < 5 minutes, it will be absorbed by the pre-warmed shoulder (no consumption of weekly 4-hour windows). We only deduct from the scheduled burst credits for sustained bursts > 5 minutes.

2) Escrow bucket billing: two options (we recommend #1 for predictability):
   - Option A (pre-pay escrow): customer prepays a burst-credit bundle; usage reduces the bundle; any overage is billed monthly.
   - Option B (post-bill): all burst usage billed monthly with a negotiated overage cap.

3) Eviction behavior & signals:
   - Preemption model: best-effort eviction for opportunistic GPUs; tasks are SIGTERM with a 30s grace; we flush KV cache where possible and attempt last-token delivery for active streams.
   - Application signals: we surface an HTTP 429 with X-Redwood-Throttle: <reason-code> when we start shedding; we also send a webhook to the registered ops endpoint if configured.
   - Fallback SLOs: we guarantee route-level failover to fallback-quantized variant within 20s for chat-style calls; for batch jobs we provide task-level retry windows of 180s.

I’ve updated the runbook to call out these signals (see capacity_runbook_v2.xlsx tab "Eviction & Signals"). If helpful, I can run a 30-min ops walkthrough on Tuesday 10:00–10:30am PT.

Regards,

Appreciate the fast feedback — summary and next steps below.

Summary of agreed points:
- Heliogenics elects Option A (pre-pay escrow). Redwood will provide a CSV credit export each invoice cycle with per-window detail.
- Eviction signal behavior: 429 + X-Redwood-Throttle + webhook; separate SLA crediting for preemption vs. hardware failure will be included in the SLA draft.
- Autoscale policy: absorb sub-5-minute bursts via pre-warmed shoulder; scheduled 4-hour windows are preserved for sustained spikes.
